newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr recoils from ugly data, but options aid.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr recoils from ugly data, but options aid.

text.p: The Australian dollar recoiled in the face of frightful jobs figures Thursday, but rumours of massive options support prevented a break of 18-month lows.

For the second month in a row the data drew a chorus of concern from analysts, dismayed employment had not responded to the 200 basis points of easing already delivered. The conclusion was the Reserve Bank had little alternative but to cut again.
"Today's unemployment report makes depressing reading," said Andrew Pease, chief economist at Nomura Australia, summing up the sentiment for all die-hard dollar bulls.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the dollar was off the floor at US$0.7425/30 having reeled as low as US$0.7410 after the figures dragged it from an early US$0.7440/45.
It finished Wednesday at US$0.7435/40 and under pressure as concerns about the figures wore away an offshore rally which had carried it to a US$0.7493 high at one point.

Dealers were surprised it had not dived further and reported good bids in the US$0.7410/20 area rumoured to be related to a huge strangle option position. "There's lots of wild talk a Chinese name is protecting a monster position -- it's supposed to be the biggest strangle ever written," said one.
Traders treated the talk with suspicion but it was enough to keep an already short market cautious of selling further.
They were not sure the reluctance would last for long once offshore investors clapped eyes on the jobs data.

The notoriously volatile employment measure rose just 11,900 in June whereas analysts had counted on a bounce of around 40,000 to correct the shock 40,300 drop seen in May. The breakdown was worse with full-time jobs actually down by 16,900 in June, making a drop of 63,900 in the last six months.
The single bright spot was a dip in the unemployment rate to 8.5 percent from 8.8 percent in May.
But even this was tarnished as the improvement came largely as a result of people giving up looking for work.
The discouragement effect saw the participation rate -- the labour force expressed as a percentage of the population aged 15 and over -- fall to a three year low of 63.0 from 63.2.
Since the RBA's charter expressely commits it to maintaining full employment, the money market concluded it would have no option but to ease policy to get the economy moving.
The 90-day bank bill future for September climbed nine basis points to a contract high of 94.99 as a result, almost entirely pricing in a 0.50 point cut in the 5.50 percent cash rate.

Bonds yields tumbled along the curve with the 10-year bond off 11 basis points to 6.62 percent, its lowest level since February 1994. The spread over 10-year U.S. Treasuries contracted to just 37 basis points, a 16-year trough.

There was a risk the RBA could ease as soon as Friday -- rumours in the futures market favoured a 75 basis point cut at the regular 9.30 am window -- but most analysts felt the central bank would not want to be seen reacting to bad economic data.
That might smack of panic and prove counter productive for consumer sentiment, particularly if the media portrayed it as a move born of desperation.
Instead, most thought the bank would wait for consumer price and wages data on July 23 and 24, which were expected to show inflation falling even further, and link an easing to this.
"The only factors which could now prevent the RBA from easing further would be excessive A$ weakness or surprisingly strong June quarter wages growth," said Nomura's Pease.

If their calculation were correct and the bank cut it would take official rates below those in the U.S. This would be an almost unprecedented event and dealers feared offshore investors would respond with their feet, as many have been doing since the last easing caught the market by surprise on May 23.

The dollar had been holding at 78 cents before then, meaning it had fallen almost five percent since. It also breached major technical levels in the process and chart watchers were looking for a retreat to 73 cents whether the bank eased or not.
The truly bearish noted that if the bank did move this month the market could well start to price in a sixth easing, a development which would threaten to return the dollar to 70 cents by year-end.
On the crosses the local currency slipped to 80.63/73 yen from 80.90/00 late here Wednesday and to 56.6 in trade weighted terms from 56.8. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
